stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a 1904 play. Mr. Pell, an amateur bird collector, has just shown his niece Agnes a drawer of mounted warblers.
PELL: There, every one labeled. Thou canst not know a bird till thou hast it in hand.
AGNES: And what hast thou learned of it, Uncle, save the colour of its coat? This one sang at dawn from the alder, I'd wager, and fed its young on midges. If the drawer holds only feathers, then all the bird's life went out of it with its breath. Ere you take another, sit an hour by the marsh and watch.
choices: Agnes argues that a mounted specimen shows how a bird looked but reveals little about how it lived.
Agnes comes to accept that a bird must be collected and labeled before it can be properly studied.
Agnes asks her uncle to explain what the warblers' feathers have taught him about their coloring.
Agnes argues that collecting warblers should be forbidden because it threatens the marsh's birds.
explanation: Put Agnes's lines into plain English: a drawer of skins tells you only the bird's color, while its singing, feeding and raising of young are lost when it dies. Her conditional ('If the drawer holds only feathers, then...') and her advice to watch living birds both make one point: specimens show appearance, not behavior. That claim covers everything she says.

B.why: This is Pell's position, not Agnes's. You matched the other character's line, and Agnes rejects that view instead of accepting it.

C.why: You read 'what hast thou learned of it' as a real question. It is rhetorical: Agnes means he has learned almost nothing, so she is not actually asking for an explanation.

D.why: Agnes asks her uncle to watch before he collects again. She never calls for a ban or says the marsh's birds are under threat, so this choice claims more than the text supports.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in an English weaving village in 1822. Mr. Cartwell, a mill owner, has told the hand weaver Hannah Doyle that his new power looms will free weavers from their toil.
HANNAH: Free us, sir? Aye, free us of our bread. If your engine weaves in a day what I weave in a week, then who will pay me for the other six days? You call it relief. But a weaver relieved of her loom is only a woman with empty hands and a hungry family.
choices: Hannah argues that power looms will strip hand weavers of their income instead of easing their labor.
Hannah agrees that power looms will spare hand weavers the long hours their work currently demands.
Hannah asks Cartwell to explain how he plans to pay weavers for the days the new looms stand idle.
Hannah argues that power looms will ruin the mill because machine-woven cloth is poorer than hers.
explanation: The introduction tells you Hannah is answering Cartwell's claim that the looms will free weavers. Her conditional ('If your engine weaves in a day what I weave in a week, then who will pay me...') and the 'But' sentence turn that claim around: the looms will take away weavers' livelihood rather than bring them relief.

B.why: This summarizes Cartwell's claim, which the introduction reports. Hannah mocks 'Free us, sir?' and rejects it, so this choice gets her position backward.

C.why: You took 'who will pay me for the other six days?' literally. Her point is that nobody will pay her. She is not asking about a payment plan, and the looms would not be the ones standing idle.

D.why: Hannah says nothing about the quality of machine-made cloth or about the mill failing. You added an argument the text never makes.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from an English translation of a nineteenth-century dialogue. A professor has just told his student Lena that regional dialects are corruptions of the standard language.
LENA: Corruptions, sir? Then was the standard never itself a dialect? Yet the speech of the capital was once a village tongue like any other, and it rose only because the court happened to sit there. If a dialect may become "correct" by the accident of where kings live, then correctness is a matter of power, not of grammar.
choices: Lena argues that the standard language owes its status to political circumstance, not superior grammar.
Lena agrees that regional dialects are flawed versions of a standard language that is more correct.
Lena asks the professor whether the language of the capital was ever regarded as a regional dialect.
Lena argues that schools should teach regional dialects in place of the standard form of the language.
explanation: Lena's conditional holds her claim: if a dialect becomes 'correct' because the court happened to sit in its region, then correctness comes from power rather than grammar. Her history of the capital's 'village tongue' supports that conclusion, so the choice that says the standard's status is political states her point.

B.why: This is the professor's view, given in the introduction. Lena's whole reply argues against it.

C.why: 'Then was the standard never itself a dialect?' is rhetorical. Lena answers it herself in the next sentence, so she is not really asking the professor anything.

D.why: Lena questions where 'correctness' comes from, but she never proposes changing what schools teach. This choice goes beyond what she says.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set aboard a trawler in 1958. The captain, Ewan Muir, has dismissed a young biologist's worry about his catch by remarking that the sea is too big to empty.
DR. SORENSEN: So said the men who fished the old cod banks, Captain. The sea is wide, I grant you, but a shoal is not. Your nets go where the fish gather to spawn. If you take them before they breed, then it matters little how many miles of water lie beyond your boat.
choices: Sorensen argues that the ocean's size cannot protect a fish population that is caught before it breeds.
Sorensen accepts that the ocean is too vast for fishing to seriously reduce the number of its fish.
Sorensen recounts how fishermen on the old cod banks once boasted about the size of their catches.
Sorensen argues that commercial fishing should be stopped until all of the cod banks have recovered.
explanation: Sorensen grants a small concession ('The sea is wide, I grant you') and then moves to her real point with 'but a shoal is not.' Her conditional finishes the argument: if fish are caught before they spawn, the size of the ocean makes no difference. The ocean's size does not protect a population fished at its spawning grounds.

B.why: This is the captain's remark from the introduction. Sorensen grants only that the sea is wide, then rejects his conclusion. You treated her concession as her claim.

C.why: The cod-bank fishermen come up in one clause, as a warning example that they once said what Muir says now. The text never mentions them boasting about catches, and the example is not her main point.

D.why: Sorensen warns about catching fish before they breed but never proposes stopping commercial fishing. This choice is a stronger claim than she makes.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set on a merchant ship in 1912. Captain Rourke has insisted that his crew is well fed, since the men have all the salted beef and ship's biscuit they want and none ever goes hungry.
DR. ABARA: Hunger is not the measure, Captain. A man may eat his fill each day and still sicken, if what he eats lacks what the body needs. Look at Hollis: his belly is full, yet his gums bleed and his old scars have opened. The body is starving long before the stomach complains.
choices: Dr. Abara argues that eating enough food does not ensure a person is getting the nourishment the body needs.
Dr. Abara agrees that the crew is healthy because the men have as much beef and biscuit as they want.
Dr. Abara argues that the salted beef itself is to blame for causing the illness that Hollis is suffering.
Dr. Abara notes that bleeding gums and reopened scars are the earliest signs that a sailor feels hungry.
explanation: The introduction gives you the captain's measure: nobody is hungry. Dr. Abara rejects that measure ('Hunger is not the measure'), and her conditional says a man can eat his fill and still get sick if his food lacks what the body needs. Hollis is her single example, and her last sentence sums up the argument: a full stomach is not proof of good nourishment.

B.why: This is Captain Rourke's position, taken from the introduction. Dr. Abara disputes it in her first sentence.

C.why: Dr. Abara says the diet lacks something the body needs, not that the beef actively causes harm. Blaming the beef goes further than her words support.

D.why: You focused on the Hollis detail and got it wrong. Dr. Abara says these symptoms appear even though he is not hungry, so they are not signs of hunger. She uses them to show his body is starving while his stomach is full.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a 1911 play. Margery Thorne, who owns a country estate, plans to drain the marsh that borders it. Her steward, Hollis, responds.

MARGERY: The marsh yields nothing. Drain it, and we shall have forty acres of good wheat by the harvest after next.
HOLLIS: Nothing, ma'am? And where do you suppose the herons feed, or the pike breed that your tenants take from the river each spring? Drain the marsh, and the river grows poorer, and so do they. Wheat you may have, but you will pay for it in fish.
choices: Hollis believes the marsh is unproductive land that would be better used for growing wheat.
Hollis argues that the marsh supports wildlife and food that the tenants depend on, so draining it has a cost.
Hollis admits he does not know where the herons feed and asks Margery to find out before she acts.
Hollis insists that wheat will not grow on the drained marsh, so the plan to plant it there will fail.
explanation: Put Hollis's lines into plain English. His question 'Nothing, ma'am?' rejects Margery's claim that the marsh yields nothing. He then points out that the marsh feeds herons and is where the pike breed, and that the tenants rely on those fish. His last sentence sums it up: she can have her wheat, but she will lose the fish. So his point is that draining the marsh has a real cost.

A.why: You summarised Margery's line, not Hollis's. She is the one who calls the marsh useless. Hollis speaks to argue against her.

C.why: You read a rhetorical question as a real one. Hollis knows perfectly well where the herons feed. He asks the question to show Margery that the marsh is not worthless.

D.why: Hollis says the opposite: 'Wheat you may have.' He agrees the wheat will grow. His objection is about what it will cost.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a 1934 play. After a dry summer, Mayor Danforth proposes digging new wells for his town. Ruth Akers, the county surveyor, replies.

DANFORTH: Three new wells, and this town need never fear a dry August again.
AKERS: Three new straws in the same glass, Mr. Mayor. The water beneath us is one body, and every well drinks from it. Had this summer's rains failed us with four wells instead of one, would the glass have been any fuller? Dig if you wish, but you will only empty it faster.
choices: Akers wonders whether the summer rains will return in time to refill the town's single well.
Akers recommends that the new wells be dug much deeper than the mayor had originally planned.
Akers agrees that adding wells will protect the town from running short of water in a dry August.
Akers argues that new wells cannot add to the town's water, since all of them draw on the same source.
explanation: Akers compares the wells to straws in one glass: every well draws from the same underground water. Her question means 'No, the glass would not have been fuller,' and her last line says more wells will just use up the water faster. So her point is that extra wells do not give the town more water.

A.why: You took her rhetorical question literally. Akers is not asking about the weather. Her question is a way of saying that more wells would not have helped during the dry spell.

B.why: Akers never mentions how deep the wells should go. You added a recommendation the text does not contain.

C.why: This is the mayor's claim. Akers brings it up only to reject it.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in 1852. Two fossil collectors, Pell and Ostrander, are examining a slab of rock that holds the imprint of a leaf.

PELL: A fern, plainly. Mark the fronds.
OSTRANDER: Fronds, aye. But where are the spore cases? Every fern I ever pressed bore them on the leaf's underside, and this leaf is bare as a plate. Look here, at the stem's end: is that not the swelling of a seed? If it is, then thou hast found no fern at all, but a plant that only dressed like one.
choices: Ostrander suggests that the fossil may be a seed-bearing plant that only resembles a fern.
Ostrander agrees that the fossil's leafy fronds clearly show it to be an ordinary fern.
Ostrander proves that the fossil is the oldest seed-bearing plant collectors have found.
Ostrander argues that the fossil's spore cases reveal it to be a rare variety of fern.
explanation: Ostrander admits the leaf has fronds, then points out it has no spore cases, which ferns carry. He asks whether a swelling at the stem's end is a seed, and his 'If it is, then…' sentence holds his claim: it may be a seed plant that only looks like a fern. The word 'if' keeps that claim tentative, and so does choice A.

B.why: This is Pell's point. Ostrander grants that the leaf has fronds and then argues that they do not settle the question.

C.why: Ostrander only says 'if it is' a seed. He proves nothing, and he never claims the plant is the oldest of anything.

D.why: Ostrander says the leaf has no spore cases. That missing feature is his whole reason for doubting it is a fern.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a 1926 play. At a city council meeting, councilman Vance praises a low-cost design for a new river bridge. The engineer Ilse Moreau responds.

VANCE: Half the steel of the other plans, and the same span. The taxpayers will thank us.
MOREAU: Will they thank us in twenty winters, when the road salt has had its way with girders cut so thin? A bridge is not bought once, Mr. Vance. It is bought every year it stands, in paint and patching and inspection. The cheaper steel makes the dearer bridge.
choices: Moreau claims that road salt is the leading cause of damage to the city's bridges and roads.
Moreau praises the design for spanning the river with half the steel the other plans required.
Moreau argues that the design's savings will be outweighed by the cost of maintaining the bridge.
Moreau is unsure whether the city's taxpayers will still approve of the bridge in twenty years.
explanation: Moreau's opening question means the taxpayers will not be thankful once salt wears away the thin girders. She then explains that a bridge keeps costing money for as long as it stands, and her last sentence sums up her point: the cheaper steel leads to a more expensive bridge over time.

A.why: Moreau mentions salt only as a threat to this bridge's thin girders. She says nothing about it being the leading cause of damage across the city.

B.why: This is Vance's argument. Moreau answers it to disagree with it.

D.why: You took her rhetorical question literally. Moreau is not unsure. She is predicting that the taxpayers will not be thankful.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a 1903 novel. Captain Hale has just returned from charting a stretch of northern coast. The mapmaker Lindqvist plans to fill in the parts Hale could not survey.

LINDQVIST: Buyers will not pay for a chart with holes in it. I shall sketch in the inlets as they likely run.
HALE: And when some master steers by your sketch into an inlet that runs only in your imagination? A blank tells him to go carefully; a guess tells him he may go boldly. I had rather sell an honest hole than a handsome lie.
choices: Hale agrees that buyers will not pay for charts that leave parts of the coastline blank.
Hale argues that blank areas on a chart keep sailors safer than guesses that look reliable.
Hale asks Lindqvist which ship captains have already steered by the charts he has sold.
Hale insists that no chart should be sold until every part of its coast has been surveyed.
explanation: Hale's question describes a danger: a captain trusting a guessed inlet that does not exist. He then contrasts the two options. A blank makes a sailor careful, while a guess makes him confident. His last line says he would rather leave an honest gap. So his point is that blanks are safer than guesses that look trustworthy.

A.why: This is Lindqvist's reason for filling in the gaps. Hale never agrees with it. He argues against filling them in.

C.why: You took Hale's rhetorical question literally. He is not asking about real captains. He is describing what could happen if someone trusted a guessed inlet.

D.why: Hale is happy to sell a chart with an 'honest hole' in it. He objects to filling gaps with guesses, not to selling charts that are incomplete.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a 1923 play. Professor Hale, a scholar of regional dialects, is answering her student Tobias, who has complained that the villagers they are recording "speak English badly."

TOBIAS: They drop half their consonants, ma'am, and say "I be" for "I am." Surely that is mere carelessness.
HALE: Carelessness? If a whole parish drops the same consonants in the same places, generation after generation, is that the work of careless tongues? A careless man errs at random. These people err by rule, and a rule kept by thousands is no error at all. It is a grammar.
choices: Tobias argues that the villagers' speech is a careless departure from correct English.
Hale points out that the villagers drop the same consonants their parents dropped.
Hale argues that the villagers' speech follows consistent rules and so forms a grammar.
Hale claims that village dialects are older and more correct than standard English.
explanation: The introduction tells you Hale is answering Tobias's complaint, so her lines carry the point. Put them into plain English: careless mistakes happen at random, but the villagers make the same changes in the same places, generation after generation. A pattern kept by thousands of speakers is a rule, and a set of rules is a grammar. Her opening 'Carelessness?' is a rhetorical question that rejects Tobias's word. Choice C states her claim.

A.why: You summarised the wrong character. This is Tobias's view, and the whole exchange exists so that Hale can reject it. You may also have read her 'Carelessness?' literally, as if she were agreeing.

B.why: You picked a true detail that is too narrow. Hale brings up the repeated consonants only as evidence. Her point is what that consistency proves: the speech is rule-governed and counts as a grammar.

D.why: You went past the text. Hale says the dialect is a grammar and not an error. She never says it is older than standard English or more correct.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from an 1890 play. Captain Rowe intends to sail before noon. Agnes, who keeps the harbor's weather station, has been reading her barometer.

ROWE: The sky is clear as glass, woman. Not a cloud from here to the cape.
AGNES: Thou mayst trust the sky if it please thee. But the glass in my parlor has fallen since dawn, and it fell so before the gale of '78, under a sky as fair as this. Ere noon the clouds will come to match it. The sky tells thee what is; the glass tells thee what is coming.
choices: Agnes argues that the falling barometer forecasts the weather better than the clear sky does.
Rowe argues that the cloudless sky shows it is safe for his ship to sail this morning.
Agnes recalls that the gale of '78 arrived under a sky just as clear as the present one.
Agnes claims that a clear sky is usually a sign that a severe storm is on its way.
explanation: The introduction sets up the disagreement: Rowe is relying on the sky, and Agnes is relying on her barometer (the 'glass'). In modern English she says, 'Trust the sky if you like, but my barometer has been falling, and the clouds will come before noon.' Her last line sums up her point: the sky shows present conditions, and the barometer shows what is coming. Choice A states that.

B.why: You summarised the other character. Rowe makes this point, and Agnes's whole speech answers it. Her 'Thou mayst trust the sky' is a concession that leads into 'But,' not an agreement.

C.why: You picked a true detail that is too narrow. Agnes mentions the gale of '78 only as an example of the barometer warning under a fair sky. It supports her point but is not the point itself.

D.why: You turned one case into a general rule Agnes never states. She says the falling barometer signals a storm. She does not say a clear sky usually means bad weather.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a translation of a 1911 play. Bram, a fisherman, is speaking with Ilse, a naturalist who has spent several seasons studying the eels of his harbor.

BRAM: You count the eels and measure them and write it all down. Why trouble? The sea holds eels enough to feed us forever.
ILSE: Forever, you say? Then tell me why your father's nets came up heavy and yours come up light. If the sea held an endless store, would each year's catch be smaller than the last? I write it down because the numbers remember what men forget.
choices: Bram insists that the sea holds enough eels to supply his village for all time.
Ilse argues that shrinking catches show the eels are limited, as her records reveal.
Ilse notes that fishermen of Bram's generation use lighter nets than their fathers did.
Ilse warns that the harbor's eels will vanish entirely within the next few years.
explanation: Ilse answers Bram with questions, but they are not real requests for information. 'Tell me why your father's nets came up heavy and yours come up light' means 'catches are falling.' 'Would each year's catch be smaller?' means 'an endless supply would not shrink.' Her last line explains why she keeps records: they preserve a decline people would otherwise forget. Choice B states both parts of her point.

A.why: You summarised the wrong character. This is Bram's belief, and Ilse's questions are built to refute it. If you took 'Forever, you say?' as agreement, you read a rhetorical question literally.

C.why: You misread the detail. The nets 'come up light' because they hold fewer eels, not because the nets themselves are lighter. Even read correctly, this detail is only her evidence, not her point.

D.why: You claimed more than Ilse does. She says the supply is shrinking and is not endless. She makes no prediction that the eels will disappear, and she gives no timeline.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from an original play set in a cotton mill. The overseer has just announced that the spinners' wages will rise by a penny a day. Agnes, a spinner, replies.

AGNES: A penny more, you say, and we are to thank you for it. But the loaf in Fenwick's window has gone up threepence since Lady Day. If a penny comes in at the door while threepence goes out at the window, then tell me, sir, which way is the household moving? You have raised our wages and left us poorer.
choices: Agnes argues that the wage increase is smaller than the rise in bread prices, so the spinners are worse off than before.
Agnes agrees that the spinners should thank the overseer for raising their wages by a penny each day.
Agnes points out that the price of a loaf in Fenwick's window has risen by threepence since Lady Day.
Agnes argues that mill wages across the country have failed to keep pace with prices for many decades.
explanation: Put Agnes's conditional into plain English: if a penny comes in and threepence goes out, the household is going backward. Her last line says so directly: the raise has 'left us poorer.' Her point is about the gap between the two amounts. The raise is twopence smaller than the price rise, so the spinners lose ground. Choice A states that claim and covers everything she says.

B.why: You took the overseer's framing, that the spinners should be grateful, and gave it to Agnes. 'We are to thank you for it' is sarcasm, and her rhetorical question exists to reject that gratitude, not to offer it.

C.why: This is true, but it covers only one of the two amounts Agnes compares. Her point is the gap between the penny and the threepence. The bread price on its own is evidence for her point, not the point itself.

D.why: Agnes is talking about one raise, one loaf and one household since Lady Day. Nothing in her lines reaches to the whole country or to decades of wages.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from an original play set in an engraving workshop. Teodor, an apprentice, has proudly told his master, Ilse, that he cut a woodblock in two days. Cutting one usually takes six.

ILSE: Two days, and thou wouldst have me praise the speed? Pull a hundred sheets from it, then. Thy lines are cut so shallow that the ink will choke them ere the fortieth. Mine took six days and gives a thousand clean prints. Count it out, boy: which block has truly cost less labour for each sheet it yields?
choices: Ilse argues that Teodor's quicker block will give far fewer prints and so costs more labour per sheet than hers.
Ilse praises Teodor for finishing his block in two days, a third of the time her own block required.
Ilse notes that a block with shallow lines will fill with ink after it has been printed many times.
Ilse insists that apprentices should never be allowed to cut a woodblock without a master's supervision.
explanation: Translate Ilse clause by clause. Teodor's block clogs before 40 prints, and hers gives 1,000. She ends with a question that is really a claim: once you count labour per print, the six-day block is the cheaper one. Her point is the gap in output between the two blocks, which outweighs the four days he saved. Choice A states that.

B.why: You read her opening question literally. 'Thou wouldst have me praise the speed?' is a challenge, not praise. The rest of the speech argues that the speed was a false saving.

C.why: This is the reason Teodor's block fails. It is not the point Ilse is making. She uses the shallow lines to set up the comparison of 40 prints against 1,000, so this choice is too narrow.

D.why: Ilse judges one block against another. She never lays down a rule about what apprentices may do, so this claims more than her lines support.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from an original play set during an 1850s fever outbreak. A councilman has just credited the town's lime-washing of houses with keeping deaths down. Dr. Marlowe answers him.

MARLOWE: On Tanner's Lane every house was washed white, and twelve were buried. On Mill Row not one wall saw lime, yet the Row draws from the new well and lost but two. If thy whitewash saved them, sir, why did it spare the street that had none of it? Look to the water.
choices: Marlowe argues that the gap in deaths between the two streets points to the water supply rather than to lime-washing.
Marlowe agrees with the councilman that lime-washing the houses is what kept the town's deaths low.
Marlowe reports that twelve people died on Tanner's Lane even though every house there was washed.
Marlowe declares that the new well has ended the fever and that the town needs no further measures.
explanation: The introduction tells you Marlowe is answering the councilman's claim about lime-washing. He compares two streets. The washed street lost twelve and the unwashed street lost two, and the unwashed street is the one with the new well. His rhetorical question means that whitewash cannot explain why the street without it did better. 'Look to the water' names the real cause. Choice A captures that comparison and his conclusion.

B.why: This summarises the councilman's view, not Marlowe's. You may have taken 'If thy whitewash saved them' as agreement. It is the start of a rhetorical question built to knock that view down.

C.why: This is accurate, but it gives you only one side of Marlowe's comparison. His point depends on setting Tanner's Lane against Mill Row, so this choice is too narrow.

D.why: Marlowe says only that the water deserves the credit. He never says the fever is over or that nothing more should be done, and Mill Row still lost two people.

stem: Based on the text, which of the following is NOT a point Ware makes?
stimulus:
In this scene from a play set in 1721, the physician Thomas Ware urges Ann Lisle to let him inoculate her son against smallpox.

LISLE: You would put into him the very sickness I pray he never meets.

WARE: A little of it, madam, given in a quiet house, that he may be spared the whole of it in a crowded street. Mark me, I promise no miracle; a few so treated do fall gravely ill. But of a hundred children who wait, how many more shall I bury?
choices: A mild infection given under care can protect against a severe one.
Some children who are inoculated go on to become seriously ill.
Inoculation is certain to leave every treated child unharmed.
More children are likely to die if they are left uninoculated.
explanation: Ware says outright, "I promise no miracle; a few so treated do fall gravely ill." He never claims inoculation is certain to leave every child unharmed. He admits the opposite. Choice C is the one point he does not make. Each of the other three can be traced to a clause in his speech.

A.why: You read "a little of it... that he may be spared the whole of it" as Lisle's fear rather than Ware's argument. Put that clause into plain English and Ware is saying a small, controlled dose protects against the full disease, so this is a point he makes.

B.why: You may have rejected this because it seems to work against Ware's case. But he concedes it himself in "a few so treated do fall gravely ill." A speaker can grant a weakness and still argue his side, so this is a point he makes.

D.why: You took "how many more shall I bury?" as a real question Ware cannot answer. It is rhetorical. He means that more children who wait will die. This is the subtype's trap: the question form hides a plain claim, and this choice states that claim.

stem: Based on the text, which of the following is NOT a point Marsh makes?
stimulus:
In this scene from a play set in an 1890s textile town, the weaver Edith Marsh answers the mill owner Samuel Crane, who has refused a wage increase.

CRANE: Raise wages, and I must raise prices; raise prices, and the buyers go to Leeds.

MARSH: Then how came you by six new looms this spring, sir, if there's no money in the till? I'll grant a mill must sell cheap. But a girl who leaves takes her skill to Leeds as surely as your buyers would.
choices: The mill recently found money to spend on new equipment.
Higher wages would push up prices and drive buyers away.
A mill has to keep the price of its cloth low to compete.
Workers who leave carry their skills to competing mills.
explanation: The claim that higher wages would push up prices and lose buyers belongs to Crane. It is his "if... then" chain in the first speech. Marsh is answering that argument, not making it, so B is not a point Marsh makes. The other three choices each paraphrase a sentence of her reply.

A.why: You took "how came you by six new looms...?" as a sincere request for information. It is rhetorical. Marsh is pointing out that the mill did have money to spend. This is the subtype's trap: a question that is really a claim.

C.why: You assumed that only the owner would say a mill must sell cheap, so you credited this line to Crane. Marsh concedes it herself in "I'll grant a mill must sell cheap" before she turns with "But." A concession is still a point the speaker makes.

D.why: You may have read "Leeds" as part of Crane's worry about buyers and stopped there. Marsh turns his own image around: a worker who leaves takes her skill to Leeds just as the buyers would. This is a point she makes.

stem: Based on the text, which of the following is NOT a point Imari makes?
stimulus:
In this scene from a play, the city planner Rosa Imari responds to Councilman Lyle Brandt, who supports building a highway through the Eastgate district.

BRANDT: The road will carry forty thousand cars a day. That is progress you can count.

IMARI: Count them, then. But count too the shops whose doors will face a wall, and the children who must cross six lanes to reach school. I do not say the city needs no road. I say that if we measure progress only in cars, we will build a city easy to drive through and hard to live in.
choices: The road would harm the shops that sit along its route.
The road would make some children's walk to school riskier.
Judging the road only by its traffic would mislead the city.
The city should abandon its plan to build any new road.
explanation: Imari states directly, "I do not say the city needs no road." Her objection is to measuring progress only by traffic. She is not objecting to roads in general. Choice D credits her with a position she explicitly rejects, so it is the one point she does not make.

A.why: You read "shops whose doors will face a wall" as background description rather than as part of her argument. In plain English she is saying the road would cut those shops off. That is a cost she wants counted, so this is a point she makes.

B.why: You may have tied the six lanes to Brandt's traffic figures and treated this as his detail. Imari is the one who raises the children crossing six lanes to reach school. She uses it as a danger the road would create, so this is a point she makes.

C.why: You skipped the conditional that carries her claim: "if we measure progress only in cars, we will build a city... hard to live in." This is the subtype's trap: older-sounding "if... then" phrasing hiding a simple point. This choice states that point.
